questions.question: When following a car, where should you ride in the lane?

options.text: The left portion.
The center portion.
The right portion.
The left or right portions.

questions.correctAnswerText: The center portion.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of the lane so the driver behind you can see you in their rearview mirror. Drivers look at their rearview mirrors more often than side mirrors, so this position makes you more visible.

questions.question: Is hearing protection important for motorcycle riders?

options.text: Not recommended if you have a full-face helmet.
Not recommended when riding with passengers.
Always recommended.
Not a concern for those with good hearing.

questions.correctAnswerText: Always recommended.
questions.explanation: Even with a helmet, wind and engine noise can damage your hearing. Earplugs protect your hearing while still letting you hear important sounds like car horns and sirens.

questions.question: Where should you place a load on your motorcycle?

options.text: As low as possible
As high as possible
Behind the rear axle
On one side of the motorcycle

questions.correctAnswerText: As low as possible
questions.explanation: Keep loads low and secure them in saddlebags. High loads on the back of the seat raise the motorcycle's center of gravity and affect balance. Always distribute loads equally on both sides.

questions.question: What percentage of motorcycle riders killed in crashes had been drinking?

options.text: 20 percent
40 percent
60 percent
80 percent

questions.correctAnswerText: 40 percent
questions.explanation: Studies show that nearly 40 percent of motorcycle riders killed in crashes had been drinking. Alcohol is a major cause of serious and fatal motorcycle accidents.

questions.question: What type of sign is yellow with black lettering?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert drivers to upcoming road conditions and hazards.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your reaction time to a hazard?

options.text: Always ride under the speed limit.
Cover the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing.
Pull the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Cover the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: In high-risk areas like school zones or construction zones, cover the clutch and both brakes. This reduces the time you need to react to a hazard.

questions.question: Why should motorcycle riders not rely only on mirrors?

options.text: Motorcycle mirrors are smaller than car mirrors, so you can't see as much.
Motorcycles, like cars, have blind spots.
Mirrors are never accurate.
Mirrors take your eyes off the road and should not be used.

questions.correctAnswerText: Motorcycles, like cars, have blind spots.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles have blind spots, just like other vehicles. You cannot rely only on mirrors to see what is behind you. Check your mirrors regularly and turn your head to look for traffic.

questions.question: The center of the lane collects oil. Should you avoid this area?

options.text: Should always be avoided.
Should be avoided if it is raining.
Offers the best traction in the lane.
Will allow you to ride faster than other parts of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Should be avoided if it is raining.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in the center of each lane. In dry conditions, this area usually has good traction. Avoid it when it is raining because the oil makes the surface slippery.

questions.question: When passing parked cars on your right, why should you avoid riding in the right portion of your lane?

options.text: Drivers may get out of a vehicle unexpectedly.
Car doors may open into your lane.
Pedestrians may step out from between cars.
Other motorists may think you're trying to park.

questions.correctAnswerText: Other motorists may think you're trying to park.
questions.explanation: Stay in the left portion of your lane when passing parked cars. This keeps you away from unexpected doors opening, vehicles pulling out, and people stepping from between cars.

questions.question: When preparing to pass another vehicle on the left, where should you position yourself?

options.text: Get into the right part of the lane so you can be seen in their side mirror.
Get into the left part of the lane to increase your line of sight.
Stay in the center part of the lane so you can be seen in their rearview mirror.
Weave in your lane to draw attention to yourself.

questions.correctAnswerText: Get into the left part of the lane to increase your line of sight.
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of your lane when preparing to pass. This improves your ability to see ahead and makes you more visible to drivers in the passing lane. Check your mirrors and turn your head before changing lanes.

questions.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: Front and rear brakes have equal stopping power.
The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake.
The rear brake is more powerful than the front brake.
Use only the front brake when stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake provides about 70 percent of your stopping power. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: On a long trip, you should:

options.text: Take as few rest breaks as possible.
Use caffeine or other stimulants if you feel tired.
Wear warm clothes to stay comfortable in cold and wind.
Ride more than 12 hours per day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Wear warm clothes to stay comfortable in cold and wind.
questions.explanation: Dress to protect yourself from wind, cold, and rain. Ride no more than 6 hours per day. Take rest breaks at least every 2 hours. Do not use stimulants—they cause extreme fatigue when they wear off.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, you should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Ride slower than normal.
Start braking earlier than normal.
Keep more distance from the vehicle ahead.
Avoid talking to your passenger while riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid talking to your passenger while riding.
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight, making the motorcycle respond more slowly. Ride slower, start braking sooner, and increase your following distance. Always tell your passenger about hazards or changes ahead.

questions.question: When riding, you should:

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn only your head and eyes to look through turns.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn only your head and eyes to look through turns.
questions.explanation: Look through the turn to see where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: When riding in a traffic lane, a motorcycle rider should:

options.text: Always ride in the same spot in the lane.
Change lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
Always ride in the center of the lane.
Always ride on the left side of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
questions.explanation: There is no single best lane position. Change your position based on current road and traffic conditions.

questions.question: The center of the lane often has an oily strip. You should:

options.text: Avoid the oily strip when the road is wet.
Ride only on the oily strip because it gives better grip.
Avoid the entire center of the lane.
Not worry about oil in the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid the oily strip when the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars builds up in the center of lanes. When dry, this area usually has enough grip for motorcycles. The strip is narrow enough that you can ride to either side and still be in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: If you must both brake and swerve to avoid a sudden hazard, you should:

options.text: Do one action, then the other.
Do both at the same time with extra braking pressure.
Do both at the same time, focusing mainly on swerving.
Do neither action.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: You need full traction to swerve safely. Do not brake and swerve at the same time. Instead, do one action first, then the other.

questions.question: Because motorcycles are hard to see at night, riders should:

options.text: Ride slower at night.
Use the horn repeatedly when riding at night.
Not ride at night.
Stay directly in front of another vehicle's headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride slower at night.
questions.explanation: Ride slower at night, increase your following distance, use the headlights ahead to help you see, use your high beam headlight unless you are following or meeting another vehicle, and be flexible with your lane position.

questions.question: During the day, your headlight should be:

options.text: Off.
On high beam.
On low beam.
Switching between high and low beam.

questions.correctAnswerText: On high beam.
questions.explanation: Using your high beam during the day helps other drivers see you. Use your high beam anytime you are not riding behind or toward another vehicle.

questions.question: A rectangular sign is used for:

options.text: School crossing warnings.
Railroad crossing warnings.
Stop signs.
Speed limit rules.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit rules.
questions.explanation: Rectangular signs show road rules like speed limits. They are white with black letters or symbols. Follow all rules shown on these signs.

questions.question: When being passed, do not move to the far side of your lane because:

options.text: The passing vehicle may return to your lane too soon.
You may block another vehicle from passing you.
The side closest to the passing vehicle is better.
You will feel more wind blast from the passing vehicle on the far side.

questions.correctAnswerText: The passing vehicle may return to your lane too soon.
questions.explanation: When being passed, do not ride on the far side of your lane. This may encourage the other driver to return to your lane before it is safe to do so.

questions.question: What formation is best for a group of riders going through a curve?

options.text: Pyramid
Staggered
Single-file
Compressed

questions.correctAnswerText: Single-file
questions.explanation: Use a single-file formation when taking curves, turning, or entering or leaving a highway. A staggered formation is better for normal group riding.

questions.question: When braking, you should:

options.text: Use the front brake first, then the rear.
Use the rear brake first, then the front.
Use both brakes at the same time.
Use the brakes in any order.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: Always use both brakes together whenever you slow down or stop.

questions.question: When entering a turn, a rider should:

options.text: Speed up.
Slow down.
Lean their shoulders to match the turn's angle.
Sit as upright as possible.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down.
questions.explanation: Before entering a turn, slow down by releasing the throttle and using both brakes if needed.

questions.question: Motorcycle headlights are:

options.text: Usually stronger than car headlights.
Usually as strong as car headlights.
Usually weaker than car headlights.
Usually larger than car headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually weaker than car headlights.
questions.explanation: Motorcycle headlights are generally smaller and weaker than car headlights.

questions.question: Which action helps you ride safely on slippery surfaces?

options.text: Using only the front brake
Using both brakes
Using the center lane
Going faster or maintaining speed

questions.correctAnswerText: Using both brakes
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, reduce speed, use both brakes, and avoid sudden movements. Stay out of the center of the lane and follow tire tracks left by cars. Watch for hazards like oil spots and loose gravel.

questions.question: Under ideal conditions, the minimum following distance should be:

options.text: One second.
Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.

questions.correctAnswerText: Two seconds.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, keep at least two seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. Increase this distance if conditions are poor.

questions.question: The center of a lane:

options.text: Is always the best place for a motorcycle.
May have oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
May have oil and grease, and is never safe for riding.
Is the smoothest part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: May have oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in the center of each lane. Unless the road is wet, this area usually has enough grip for motorcycles. Avoid large oil buildups at busy intersections and toll booths.

questions.question: When preparing to pass on the left, ride on the left side of your lane because:

options.text: The right side may be slippery.
It gives you a better view of hazards in the next lane.
Drivers don't expect to be passed on their left.
It places you in the car's rearview mirror.

questions.correctAnswerText: It gives you a better view of hazards in the next lane.
questions.explanation: Riding in the left portion of your lane improves your sight line and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic when preparing to pass.

questions.question: If a passing vehicle's wind blast hits you, you will have the most space to recover if you are riding:

options.text: In the left portion of the lane.
In the center portion of the lane.
In the right portion of the lane.
On the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center portion of the lane.
questions.explanation: Riding in the center of your lane gives you the most room to move if a wind blast affects your control.
